transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-07 16:30 UTC | Duration: ~52 minutes | Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Lena Cho (Redwood SE), Oliver Hayes (CTO, Lumina), Maya Singh (ML Eng), Rita Gomez (PM)

Summary (auto): quick demo of Redwood structured output features incl JSON mode, function/tool calling, Console walkthrough and Optimize suggestions; customer questions about guardrails, validation, private deployment and SSO/keys; agreed next steps to share notebook and security docs and follow up on POC.

[00:00] Samir: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Quick intros, I'll hand to Lena to run the demo — we're going to show structured output (JSON mode), function/tool calling and how the Console + Optimize suggest tradeoffs.
[00:18] Lena: Hi all, Lena Cho, SE at Redwood. We'll start with an API example then jump into the Console where you can set schemas and guardrails and then a short Optimize tour.
[00:30] Oliver: Sounds good. We're most interested in deterministic JSON output for downstream ingestion — our pipeline breaks if fields are missing.
[00:40] Maya: And we want to call internal tools securely, i.e. model decides when to call a function to fetch patient metadata — but data can't leak.
[00:55] Lena: Totally. We'll demo JSON mode that emits a strict schema and the function-calling layer which maps to your microservices. Note: function calling here is Redwood's tool calling feature, same idea as function-call in other providers, but integrated with the Console policies.

[01:22] Lena: Opening the Console — here you can upload a JSON schema or compose it inline. For example we define a patient_summary object with required fields: id, last_seen_iso, risk_score (float) and notes (string). You can set field-level validators and mark fields as redacted if they should never be stored.
[01:45] Speaker 1: I see the schema pane; is there automatic validation on generation?
[01:54] Lena: Yes, we run a post-generation validator and can configure hard vs soft validation. Hard validation rejects responses that don't conform; soft will surface warnings and optionally trigger a fallback model or a re-prompt. For mission-critical pipelines we recommend hard validation plus a canary route so bad outputs go to a safe model variant.

[02:30] Maya: How does it handle partially missing fields? For example the model can't infer risk_score.
[02:38] Lena: Two options: use a default sentinel (we support nulls and default values) or annotate the schema with a 'confidence_required' flag which forces a tool call to your scoring service.

[03:05] Oliver: About guardrails and PII — can we prevent PHI from leaving the VPC during function calls?
[03:12] Samir: For Redwood Private we support customer-managed networking and egress controls; function calls can be routed to internal endpoints only. Also KMS integration for keys, and audit logs. We'll share the security kit.

[03:40] Lena: Back to the demo — I'll run a live generation. Endpoint: POST /v1/generate with mode=json and schema attached. (typing, simulated output)
[04:00] [live run noise, some typing sounds]
[04:15] Lena: Example response: {"patient_summary": {"id": "p-324", "last_seen_iso": "2025-04-06T13:22:00Z", "risk_score": 0.78, "notes": "follow up in 2 weeks"}} — note the response is strictly shaped. We also show a validation log: PASS.
[04:40] Maya: Nice. If the model hallucinated and produced extra keys, would validation strip them or fail?
[04:50] Lena: You can choose: strict mode will fail the call; permissive will strip unknown fields. For audit we log both the raw model text and the validated payload.

[05:10] Lena: Now function calling: we declare a function in the Console, map its signature to your service, and the model will return a 'call' signal with arguments matching your schema. Redwood's runtime will then execute the call (optionally in your VPC) and stream the result back into the model context.
[05:37] Oliver: So the model never directly sees the raw DB credentials, right?
[05:44] Lena: Correct — credentials are stored in your KMS/HSM and the runtime handles the invocation. We can do signed short-lived tokens for the call broker.

[06:05] Speaker 2: How do you ensure the model calls the function only when appropriate?
[06:12] Lena: We use schema-driven function signatures and few-shot examples to teach the model. Also Console has a 'calling threshold' — confidence below threshold falls back to a clarification or a safe handler.

[06:40] Maya: Can we run the demonstration against our dev model, like a smaller quantized variant? Latency matters for us.
[06:48] Samir: Yes, Redwood supports model variants and routing policies. In Dedicated mode you can pin quantized models for throughput. Optimize will recommend quantization + batching settings based on your latency budget.

[07:10] Lena: Switching to the Optimize screen — this is where we show token-level cost, suggested batch sizes, and quantization profiles by workload. For a high qps low-latency path we might recommend int8 quantization and small batch sizes, plus KV cache for repeated prompts.
[07:35] Oliver: Any metrics on how structured output affects token costs?
[07:42] Lena: Structured output may slightly increase token usage if you ask for verbose schemas, but using pre-defined templates and prefix caching reduces repeated tokens. Optimize shows per-route cost deltas and simulated cost under different configs.

[08:10] Lena: Demo: function call flow. Model decides to call get_patient_history({id: p-324}). Console shows the call payload, the execution (routed to Lumina's dev endpoint in our demo), and the returned JSON, which the model then uses to fill patient_summary.
[08:32] [short pause]
[08:36] Rita: If the function returns malformed JSON, what happens?
[08:40] Lena: The runtime attempts best-effort parsing; if it fails the validator can mark false and trigger fallback. We also provide middleware hooks so your service can return a standardized envelope that we validate server-side before it enters the model context.

[09:05] Maya: On rate limits and quotas — can we throttle function call rates per route?
[09:12] Samir: Yes, per-route throttling, quotas, and circuit breakers. Important for 3rd-party services.

[09:30] Speaker 1: Are there examples for multi-step workflows? e.g., tool A then B then produce final JSON.
[09:38] Lena: We support multi-call sequences; each call's output can be appended to the context and subsequent decisions are made by the model. The Console lets you visualize the call graph. Beware of context growth — Optimize suggests summary + caching policies.

[10:05] Oliver: Security checklist items — SSO, role-based access, audit logs, data residency. Do you have compliance docs?
[10:13] Samir: We'll send the SOC2, ISO, and a private deployment checklist. For SSO we support SAML/Okta and fine-grained RBAC.

[10:30] Lena: A quick note about streaming: structured output can stream but validators run progressively — we support schema-first streaming where fields are emitted in order and validated as they come. It's helpful for low-latency UIs.

[10:55] Maya: Does streaming complicate function calling?
[11:00] Lena: It can; for streaming we often recommend doing critical calls up-front or using a hybrid: initial call to fetch deps then stream final partial outputs. Console has patterns for that.

[11:22] [demo continues with a noisy terminal click and brief lag]
[12:05] Lena: Showing the API snippet: Node + Python examples. For Python: client.generate(mode='json', schema=..., functions=[...], stream=True). Responses arrive as a validated JSON object event.
[12:28] Speaker 2: Any SDK locks to vendor? Can we bring our own model weights?
[12:35] Samir: In Private deployments you can bring models; Dedicated supports pinned VMs and image builds. The SDK is standard REST/HTTP so vendor lock is low.

[13:02] Oliver: About observability — if validation fails in production how do we trace back?
[13:09] Lena: Each request has a trace id, token breakdown, and validation logs accessible in Console. We also provide hooks to export traces to Datadog/ELK.

[13:30] Rita: What about costs for POC? Any credits or trial?
[13:36] Samir: We typically provide trial credits and a short POC engagement. For larger data-sensitive POCs we can run a private demo env. We'll detail in the pricing packet.

[14:00] [customer side murmur; brief cross-talk]
[14:18] Oliver: Two concerns — auditability and fallback when model degrades after an update.
[14:25] Lena: We support pinned model versions and rollout controls (canary, A/B). Optimize adds regression detection tied to eval sets; if quality drops, automatic rollback or route to a safe model.

[14:50] Lena: Quick walkthrough of schema editor again — you can add enumerations, regex validators, numeric ranges and opt into encryption on certain attributes.
[15:10] Maya: Nice. For numeric precision (risk_score), we need consistent formatting. Is that handled?
[15:18] Lena: Yes, schema types include number with format directives. We also post-process to enforce decimal places.

[15:40] Speaker 1: How do you handle training data leakage concerns? If a model memorized PHI could it echo?
[15:48] Samir: We encourage private deployment for sensitive workloads; additionally Console can redact fields and we have tokenization policies and can filter sensitive substrings before storage/telemetry. We'll send the memo with examples.

[16:10] [brief pause]
[16:18] Lena: Demo wrap-up: example end-to-end flow produced a validated patient_summary, executed two function calls, and recorded trace + validation passes.

[16:35] Oliver: This looks promising. Next steps: we'll review the security docs and figure out the POC scope.
[16:42] Samir: Great. We'll send the notebook and pricing. Any blockers on your side for a 2-week POC?
[16:50] Maya: Need to confirm internal legal and data access but should be doable.

[17:05] Rita: Can you provide sample schemas for other endpoints (medication, visits)?
[17:12] Lena: Yes, I'll include templates in the notebook.

[17:30] Samir: Recap of action items and owners: I'll send pricing and SOC2 by Thursday; Lena will share the demo notebook and schema templates by Wednesday; Maya will provide example payloads by Friday.

[17:50] Oliver: Thanks everyone.
[17:54] Lena: Thanks, we'll follow up in email and add the POC kickoff link.

[18:05] End meeting.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker mislabels and minor recognition errors (e.g., 'Redwood Dedicate' vs Dedicated) present. References shared: demo notebook link (shared privately), security packet (link), pricing spreadsheet (link).
